title: Citizenship in Heaven (Philippians 3:1–21)
transcript: Uh, we're in our Philippians series, we're now in chapter 3, and we're continuing with this little booklet, Mind the Gap. I told today that we've run out of these, but they are available online, and it will help you to follow up what I say today and to do some devotional work in the passage as well. Last week I was trying to think of a situation in mathematics where you could add two numbers together but end up with less than you began with? And the answer to my dilemma lay in taking a positive number and adding a negative number to it. So 5 plus minus 3 is 2, not 7. I know it's a simple Key Stage 2 mental arithmetic problem. But Paul, as he writes this thanksgiving letter to the Philippians, has a Key Stage 2 mathematics problem that he too is trying to resolve. Having launched his mission to the mostly Greek-speaking believers, certain people have appeared among them telling them that they must add something to their newfound faith. "Unless you are circumcised," they say, "you cannot be saved." And Paul's first response is to ask them why. Why do they want to test God by putting a yoke on the Gentiles? On the necks of God's people that they have never been able to bear? Isn't it enough that the Gentiles have come to believe in the Lord Jesus and received the Holy Spirit just as the Jewish believers had? But now, as he writes this letter, he goes further in confronting them as a protection to those in Philippi. He warns his listeners that adding anything to their faith in Jesus will not just diminish it, but will bring it to nothing. Indeed, he argues Christ plus anything will mean the destruction of that relationship. It is utterly fatal. In our meet and greet, we asked you, what is the most exclusive place you have ever been? At the start of Wimbledon week, perhaps the it is the hallowed lawns of SW1. But for the Christian, the most exclusive place that you can ever be is in Christ. Nothing can be added to that experience of him that doesn't ruin it. Nothing can be added to the good news about him that doesn't create a different message. You cannot cling to him and to someone or something else without losing what you sought. So Paul feels it necessary to warn the church not to add anything to basic faith. For us, it's probably not the inclination towards gospel surgery as the circumcisers in this passage are demanding, but there are all sorts of props that we might use to support our faith and to give us greater assurance. Or things that people might insist on to include us in their particular flavor of Christianity. But Paul's appeal is for a plain vanilla version of the gospel truth. Our confidence is to rest in Christ alone. Well, that's the broad field of discovery laid out for us this morning. So let's have a look how Paul addresses his mathematical problem within the passage itself. And Paul begins this section of his letter with a warning. And I have lost my clicker, but Tim can help me out. There we go. Actually, it is a bit of a weird warning, for its opening words are to rejoice, to rejoice in the Lord. Some of you will know my Presbyterian background, and that reminded me of the story of a rather dour Presbyterian lady who, after the sermon, came up to the preacher and said, "You know, Mr. Smith, you were so funny this morning, I almost smiled." Sometimes Christians are not well known for their joyfulness. But 6 times in this letter, Paul encourages the church to be joyful. In chapter 1, they are to rejoice whether the gospel is preached from good motives or bad, for what matters is preached. And in chapter 2, Paul asks them to rejoice in their sacrifice and their giving, which has come from their faith in Christ. And in chapter 4, he rejoices in their concern for him. And his point overall is that whatever their circumstance Christians find themselves in, that they should rejoice because the Lord is is at work in it and through it. So here again, the Philippians are told to rejoice, to rejoice in the Lord. Jesus is to be both the basis and the focus of our joy. He is to be at the heart of everything that we do. So naturally, Paul's warning arises from this concern at Philippi. They must not do anything that would displace the lordship, the centrality of Jesus in their lives. And the example Paul turns to is the issue that has dogged his own ministry. It is those who insist that non-Jewish believers must tick extra boxes if they are to become a genuine part of the of God's people. Specifically, they are demanding that the Gentile believers become circumcised. While the problem may not be present in Philippi just yet, nevertheless Paul warns against this practice with considerable force. And to be honest, the NIV feels a little bit timid in its translation here. It certainly doesn't convey the literary punch that's present in the original. For 3 times Paul tells them to beware, beware. And if you can forgive me a little mistranslation of my own, it says something like this: Beware the canines, beware the crooks, beware the 'Beware the cutters.' Paul is trying to subvert these Jews and the claims that they make on the Gentile believers. Jews who would demean the Gentiles as dogs, as something impure and on the margins of society, something you might kick as you walk by. But now it is they whom Paul likens to dogs. And those Jews who would have thought of themselves as God's people, as being inherently good, Paul now inverts that by calling them the wicked. And those who bear the sign and seal of God's covenant, the visible mark of the promises of Abraham, are no longer those who 'who have had their foreskins cut, but they have cut them to pieces.' Well, that may well make you wince at that point. It does seem, at the least, a little ungracious. But it did remind me of when Jesus confronted Peter and rebuked him, saying, 'Get behind me, Satan.' It is a measure of the gravity of the situation. That in limiting Jesus' ministry, Peter was undermining the whole mission of Jesus, the good news that would flow from it. And in the same way, Paul is making his point very strongly, which is now that Jesus has come, the identity of God's people must lie solely in him. The symbols of the promise are no longer law and circumcision, but Jesus. And so to insist on the previous markers of true faith, that they be retained, only diminishes Jesus' position. And actually, it negates it completely, for you can only trust in one thing. And that is not to say that circumcision was wrong or that Jewish believers now needed some kind of revision surgery. It is just that now, but that belongs to, all of that is in a different age, in a different covenant. That is where it belongs. And faith in Christ, faith in Christ alone is now all that matters. And so, as Paul now claims in verse 3, if you have a look, it is we who are the circumcision—Jew and Gentile believers together under Christ. It is we who serve God by his Spirit, just as it was promised by the prophets about this new age. And therefore, it is we who must boast in Jesus. Rather than in the flesh. That is where the believer's confidence now lies. And the flesh is being used, I think, here in several senses. Euphemistically, it is pointing to circumcision as the covenant mark made in the flesh. But more generally, it is used to mean that they should not put their confidence 'in any physical, earthly, or fleshy thing'—in fact, in anything that is not Christ. We could look to an infinite number of things to provide our joy, our security, our worth, but ultimately trust in Christ is our only hope. For the Christian, that is where your confidence must lie. Well, I am going to have a little test of memory now, as well as a quick drink so that I don't pass out. When Trev was preaching several weeks ago, he said that Paul has written the book of Philippians to teach you how to— Wow, sermons don't work, do they really? Can anybody remember what he said? Trevor said it is to teach you how to— Gaze, yes, thank you, we're there. Someone, one person was listening, excellent. Teach you how to gaze. Paul's inviting you into his picture gallery so that you might gaze at the images, so that you might acquire the character of a gospel person. And some of those pictures, as we have seen, have been self-portraits. So today we have 3 more pictures to gaze upon, which David Turner helpfully named for me. And they are, if you can put them on the screen for me, the accountant, the athlete, and the alien. And each of them is a snapshot of what it means to live with Christ in first place and so find joy in our Christian walk. So we begin then with the accountant. Just when you thought we had got rid of all the mathematics from the sermon. And the danger that Paul sees is that the believers may be pressured to add something to their faith in Christ so that they can some kind of pedigree or performance in order to prove it genuine and to be accepted. But what Paul sees is that if it's about having the right credentials, then he is the perfect card-carrying Jew. He has it all. He's circumcised. He's a Jew born and bred. He has royal heritage, a son of Saul. Related to the first king of Israel, born in the tribe of Benjamin. He has all the pedigree that anyone could ask for. But Paul also has performance. He's not only lived under the law faultlessly as a Jew, but as a Pharisee, he has taught the law. And if religious zeal is the measure of belonging in the club, then he is someone who has persecuted the church, not just enforced its dress code. So if anyone wants to do the financials, Paul's bank balance is firmly in the black. Everything is in his favor. And it made me wonder what we might list as the essential elements of being accepted as a card-carrying evangelical. It's worth considering, isn't it? And yet, when Paul tots up all the gains in his spreadsheet, what he realises is that his bank balance is not in the black at all. It is actually in the red. Verse 7: 'Whatever were gains to me, I now consider loss for the sake of Christ.' Or verse 8: 'I consider everything a loss because of the surpassing worth of Christ Jesus.' of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. Everything that Paul has invested his life into has added nothing to his standing before God. Indeed, it's adding with a negative number. It has reduced his overall standing. And so rather dramatically, he declares that it's all garbage. And it's garbage because if the goal is to be in a proper relationship with God, then no symbols or honours or achievements or position or status will ever deliver that, but only faith, a lived-out trust with Jesus Christ. There have been quite a few stories in the news recently about stolen valour. You know those people who turn up at military events wearing a chest full of medals they never earned? But look, you can pin as many bits of tin on your chest as you like, but it will never make you a soldier. For Paul, adding symbols is pointless as they won't change who you are, but faithful trust will. And it's this basic trust that has enabled him to joyfully join in Jesus with his suffering, to aspire to be like him in his death, and to hope in the power of the resurrection as the ultimate vindication that he will not have lost everything to gain nothing. Well, then our second picture we get to gaze on is the athlete. Fear not, these legs, these Irish legs are not going to make an appearance in shorts. You do not need to fear. Paul is careful here not to imply that he is some sort of superhero, one whom you could not emulate. But rather, just like the Philippians, he is a plodder. He is someone who is still jogging around the track towards the finish line. In the hope of winning the prize at the end of the race. And this running image is something that Paul has used on several occasions. To the church in Corinth, he wrote that he had learned to train and discipline himself so that he might win the prize before him and not be disqualified from the race. Or in Acts, Paul says this: I consider my life worth nothing to me for the sake of the gospel. My only aim is to finish the race and complete the task that the Lord Jesus has given me—the task of testifying to the good news of God's grace. As a runner, he has learnt discipline, he has learnt single-mindedness, and his focus is on knowing Christ and thereby making him known. And that's it. And it's towards that goal that he must now press on. And I love that little phrase that's there in verse 12, if you have a look, "I press on to take hold of that for which Christ took hold of me." It sums up so well Paul's desire to fully embrace the purpose for which Christ saved him. God's plan in Jesus is being worked out in each of our lives. And we must therefore lean into the gifts and the circumstances that he has provided to us, always moving forward in our faith, whatever stage of life we are in. For those of us who are getting a bit older, it is quite easy, isn't it, to run out of puff? But we are on this journey and we have got to keep going. And Paul is quick to add that he is not at the finish line yet. As verse 13 tells us, "I do not consider myself yet to have taken hold of it." He has not fully taken hold of what Christ took hold of him for. But again, and I love the simplicity of this next phrase, "This one thing I do." Wouldn't it be great to just have one thing to do in the Christian life? Wouldn't that make it really easy? Well, here it is. There's one thing I do: I press on. Bad day at work and want to give up? I press on. Problems in your marriage? I press on. Struggling with your friendships? I press on. Fix your eyes on Jesus. Desire to know him that others might know him also, and press on in trust with Jesus. And there are two aspects of this that Paul highlights for us here in verse 13. First is, "I forget what is behind and I strain forward to what is ahead." As someone once said, we can learn from the past but we mustn't live in the past. Nor do I think that somehow Paul has become absent-minded and forgotten his past. That he once persecuted the church. He's all too aware of that, I'm sure. But now he thinks about his past differently. Each of us has a past, but it is within that past that Christ loved us and found us and rescued us and now points us in a new direction. He's put us under new management and given us a new purpose to live for. And the conclusion that Paul reaches in verse 15 is that all of us then who are mature should take such a view of things. Each of us must strive after Christ, having put the past behind and and then strive forward to model him in our lives as an example to others. Well, our final gallery picture then is that of the alien, by which I don't mean that little green chap who has oblong eyes. Rather, we should live as a foreigner, as someone without citizenship, as someone who doesn't quite belong. As Paul closes this section, he sets out for us here two destinies that result from two different ways of living—living for today or living for tomorrow. Our eyes set on earthly things or our eyes set on heavenly things. But you can't have both. You can't look up and look down simultaneously. And so in verse 18, we have those whose confidence is in the flesh, just like those of the circumcision brigade. Their god is their stomach. Their focus is on earthly things. But in choosing that path, Paul says they deny the power of Christ and his cross for salvation. Why? Because their focus is on themselves. They trust in their own effort to deliver themselves from life's calamities. And they are controlled by powerful desires, by passions, rather than by the power of Christ. And yes, they will have their successes. They will have their day in the sun. Their glory will be everything that they have achieved and can boast about in life. But in the end, it will prove to be their shame and ultimately, verse 19, their destruction. I have taken a lot of funerals, and death is the great leveller. It's a reminder that Eventually everything goes back in the box and whatever you have achieved in life will count for nothing unless it is counted for Christ. So for the unbeliever it is glory now but death tomorrow. But not for the Christian. And the contrast here is stark. Their focus is on eternity. Their citizenship is in heaven rather than on earth. That's where they belong. That's where they feel truly at home. And they hope for Christ's return and his reign to be fully established. For Paul, this is the reason that he can suffer humility and loss joyfully, for he knows he's invested in what is to come. Rather than what is present. As Phil Alcock last week put it in his sermon, it's why godly people can make choices about houses and cars and jobs and pursuits and lifestyles and joyfully accept the lack of promotion, income, recognition, or reward. Their focus is on something else. So what does that mean? Does that mean the Christian misses out on glory? No, says Paul. When Christ returns, our lowly bodies will be transformed to be like his glorious body. They will have the prize that they have sought to gain every day, and that that is Christ. They will be perfected in his image and share in his glory. And so, to slightly misquote Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking Glass, the rule is jam tomorrow but never jam today. Well, as we end, I was reminded of a recent Airbnb advert which says this: 'Travel, it's gone from being an adventure to a checklist.' It would be a shame if that could be said about our spiritual life also. Paul's appeal to the church is to adopt a simple faith without checklists. Faith that rests in the sufficiency of Christ at all times and in all circumstances. True joy and spiritual progress therefore comes not from self-effort or worldly achievements, but from a growing relationship with Jesus Christ grounded in the hope of resurrection glory. So let's listen then to Paul's warning: put your trust in Jesus alone and follow the mature examples of Christian living that he has provided to guide us on the way. Amen. Well, as the band come up, let me pray for us. Father, thank you that we can gaze at the cross at Paul and at those ahead of us in the race and emulate their faith and their dependence on Jesus, who is our resurrection hope for salvation. Amen.
